article_text:
Prince William has declared his love for Christopher Nolan films and The Celebrity Traitors in an unexpected appearance on The Graham Norton Show.

Sitting on the BBC late-night show’s famous red sofa, the Prince of Wales told Norton that he relaxes by watching movies and listening to music.

“I love getting immersed in deep-thinking films. I like action films too, but I like something a bit different,” he told Norton during the show’s recording on Thursday.

“I’m a big fan of everything Christopher Nolan does. His films are fantastic – The Dark Knight series is psychologically dark and deep and I absolutely love that. He takes concepts that are completely out there and makes them incredibly entertaining.”

'SNL UK' Cold Open Features Face-Off Between Prince William & Harry: "Oh Look, It's The Woman From 'Suits'"

On The Celebrity Traitors , he added: “I love it, the family love it. Charlotte and Louis are obsessed with it. It’s really good telly.”

Watch on Deadline

He continued: “I saw Ross Kemp the day after the first episode and I couldn’t help but try – in the most appropriate way – to touch him to see what reaction I got from him. Turns out he was really jumpy.”

William appeared on Norton to discuss The Earthshot Prize, his environmental initiative. He said: “For many years I was hearing stories about environment issues and one thing that struck me was the negativity and doom, which got me down. I thought we could do something more powerful and more optimistic and the idea of an awards’ ceremony came about and we could talk about urgency and optimism together.”

Other guests include Cate Blanchett, Hannah Waddingham, and conservationist Robert Irwin. Singer-songwriter Jorja Smith completes the lineup.

The Graham Norton Show will air tonight on the BBC and screens on BBC America in the U.S.

article_text:
John Wilson ‘s next trick? Showing his dedicated audiences “how to” tour like Harry Styles . The “History of Concrete” filmmaker and “How to with John Wilson” creator is allegedly already hard at work on his next project: a concert documentary about Styles and his current “Together, Together” tour for Universal Pictures Content Group.

The news was first reported by Variety , but eagle-eyed social media denizens had already been sent into gossip overload after videos of Wilson following and filming Styles started to make the rounds over the weekend. IndieWire has reached out to Universal for comment.

According to Variety, Wilson has been filming Styles since August. The pop star is the midst of his latest residency at Madison Square Garden, which is poised to run through October and is the largest single-engagement residency ever at the iconic venue. Per the outlet, “Wilson is capturing footage for a doc expected to be a hybrid of live performances and a glimpse into Styles’ world. One source described it as featuring authentic human stories of everyone involved in the tour —from the singer and his fans to countless others behind the scenes.”

Variety adds that “Universal Pictures Content Group, Peanut World Pictures, and Styles produced the project. UPCG will own global rights to the film .” Distribution plans are not yet set, but “insiders said the doc may be positioned for a theatrical release via Universal.”

As Variety reminds us, while Wilson might seem like an odd choice for such a gig, he did get his start directing music videos. And concert docs are big business these days , even from lauded filmmakers, The outlet’s Matt Donnelly notes that “Billie Eilish recruited ‘Titanic’ and ‘Avatar’ mastermind James Cameron to direct her own theatrical concert opus ‘Hit Me Hard and Soft: The Tour,’ which was released in theaters this summer.”

And, remember a little film called “Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour” ?

Wilson is on a hot streak as of late, as IndieWire reported earlier this week that his first feature-length documentary, “The History of Concrete,” recently passed $2 million at the box office. We’re guessing this next one will make a smidge more.
excerpt_original: Hot off the success of his feature debut “The History of Concrete,” the beloved documentarian has turned his camera onto the pop star and his recent tour.

article_text:
Cynthia Erivo is reflecting on the attention her friendship with “ Wicked ” co-star Ariana Grande received while on the press tour for the movie musical and its sequel.

The theater star and singer has rocketed to greater heights of fame following Jon M. Chu’s adaptation of “Wicked,” which stars Erivo as the wicked witch Elphaba opposite Grande’s Glinda the Good. Many moments from the press tour for the 2024 film went viral online, and the close relationship between the stars was called into question.

Related Stories

Netflix Romance ‘Love Untangled’ Director Namkoong Sun on Netflix Freedom and the Funding and Distribution Gap in Korean Indie Film

U2 to Play Halftime Show for NFL's Thanksgiving Eve Game in What League Calls 'a New NFL Holiday Tradition'

“It was interesting that there were many people who had become psychologists from their couches,” Erivo told The Guardian during an interview for her upcoming courtroom drama “Prima Facie.” “There was this weird sort of, what’s the word I’m looking for … annoyance … at the fact that two women could actually be friends. Like, why are they friends? Why are they connected? There must be something wrong with them.”

Many viral moments included the co-stars hugging, crying and — perhaps most infamously — “holding space” by pinching each other’s pointer fingers. “Why are they showing emotion? How dare they cry? And how dare they laugh? And how dare they be emotive and alive?” Erivo asked.

“It’s a double-edged sword,” she added. “Because if we were dead behind the eyes and showing no emotion, there would have been something else to say about it. I wish there was someone who could have been like, ‘Right, this is the proper balance of emotion that you should show. Don’t show this. Don’t show that. Just this amount.’”

One of the most memorable moments happened when Erivo jumped into action after a man grabbed Grande on the red carpet in Singapore. Erivo described the moment as terrifying and said her reaction was just “‘Get this man away from us now.’”

The internet began positioning Erivo as Grande’s “bodyguard,” a description she feels uncomfortable with. She said that reaction was centered in misogyny and misogynoir. “I was like: ‘Oh, you think because I look like this that you could talk to me this way about something that was a human thing that I would have done for any friend, and hopefully a friend would have done for me,’” she said. “But I must be a bodyguard.”

title_original: Sofia Bassi’s Market Is Heating Up as Female Surrealists Get Their Due

article_text:
Sofia Bassi ’s paintings are portals. In Eclosión (1969), an eye formed of sinew and vapor bursts out of an egg, a whirling gyre reigns over ruined buildings, and a pair of skeletons make an inspection. Devise your own narrative. It’s an absurd and unsettling dreamscape, something Hieronymus Bosch might have painted in a furious mood.

Eclosión is one of 16 works by the Mexican Surrealist on display at Pippy Houldsworth Gallery , which is mounting the artist’s first European solo exhibition, “Floating Between Earth and Sky,” through November 14. The show arrives as demand for Bassi’s work reaches new highs at auction.

“There has been a surge of interest in female Surrealists.” Pippy Houldsworth said in an email. “ Leonora Carrington and Remedios Varo have become household names, both of whom Bassi associated with. Despite this, Bassi has remained largely unknown outside of Mexico. Her work more than holds up to her contemporaries.”

To further Bassi’s exposure, the gallery is also including Untitled (1969), a round landscape with Surrealist symbols, at its booth at Frieze London. The work is priced at $85,000.

Bassi, who died in 1998, at 85, only picked up the brush in her 50s. Her oeuvre grew darker between 1968 and 1972, when she was imprisoned in Acapulco after pleading guilty to the murder of her son-in-law. ( Eclosión is signed “ELC”, an abbreviation of “En la Cárcel,” Spanish for “in prison.”) Works from this period, priced between $20,000 and $400,000, form the focus of Houldsworth’s show.

Sofia Bassi, Untitled (1969). Photo: courtesy Prudence Cuming Associates Ltd / Pippy Houldsworth Gallery,

The gallery’s presentation is in partnership with Bassi’s Foundation, run by her daughter-in-law and granddaughter, and Georgina Pounds Gallery in Mexico City, an early booster that staged the largest exhibition dedicated to Bassi to date this past spring. While the foundation retains some of Bassi’s best paintings, many more are spread among Latin American private collections.

Pounds is clear about the impact of prison on Bassi’s career. In 1967, she was one of seven female artists exhibited alongside Frida Kahlo in a landmark exhibition at Mexico City’s Museum of Modern Art (MAM). A year later, she was behind bars.

“Imprisonment became inseparable from her public biography and to some extent overshadowed her practice,” Pounds said in an email. “Her work subsequently receded from dominant histories of Mexican modernism and Surrealism.”

That could be changing. In May, Mexico’s Morton auction house sold Bassi’s Muñeca Reina (1974), a fiery woodscape haunted by a long-necked girl, for a record 800,000 Mexican pesos ($46,000). An untitled work, from 1992, sold for $44,800 at Sotheby’s on October 9, doubling it’s high estimate.

According to the Artnet Price Database, Bassi’s works have sold for an average of $29,291 at auction so far in 2026, more than double the $12,897 average in 2025 and well above the $3,000 to $7,000 that was typical through the 2010s.

Earlier this year, the collector Christian Levett acquired four Bassi works from Georgina Pounds Gallery for his museum dedicated to female artists. Bassi’s works are also in the collections of the Tel Aviv Museum of Art and MAM. An institutional show, Pounds said, is in the offing.

article_text:
For writer and director Christian Everhard, “ The Crawling ” began as a late-night thought experiment. While on vacation with a girlfriend at an isolated cabin, he woke up in the middle of the night, his mind racing. As a horror fan, he started thinking about the scariest worst-case scenario. Could a dangerous local break into the house? Could an animal scurry in?

And then he saw a bright flash of light he couldn’t account for.

Related Stories

Stephen Amell Says Putting on the 'Baywatch' Red Trunks Felt 'So Familiar' Because 'It's a Superhero Show'

“The Crawling” is, indeed, about a married couple, Mike (Will Brittain, “Kong: Skull Island”) and Emma (Katherine Hughes, “Tell Me Lies”), on vacation in a remote house. One night, Mike is woken up not only by bright lights but also an alien being. Adding to his distress is the fact that Emma thinks he dreamed up the encounter. Things escalate from there, with plenty of twists, turns and extraterrestrial madness.

Popular on Variety

But what elevates “The Crawling” is not just alien scares and creature effects — although there are plenty of those, courtesy of Onyx Forge’s Steve Wang & Cleve Gunderman. As “Obsession” launched dozens of think pieces about modern dating, consent and control, “The Crawling” conjures plenty of discomfort from the increasingly fraught relationship between Mike and Emma, which might cut close to real life for many in the audience.

Everhard’s first bold choice was centering the film on a character that people might not have empathy for, as Mike’s an alpha police officer on suspension for assaulting a suspect. In a conversation I had with the director following the Oct. 23 world premiere of the film at the Provo, Utah, festival FilmQuest , he explained why Mike was the perfect protagonist, flaws and all.

“Once I figured out what was going to happen to this guy, I started to think, ‘Who would be the one that this would shatter the most?’” Everhard said. “I thought about the guy who defines himself by his manliness and masculinity — not only in his personal life, but also in his work. That started to open the door, and the more I explored it, the more I realized there was an opportunity to peel back the layers of not just gender and identity, but I became transfixed with this idea of, ‘What if I started the film with this guy that the audience probably won’t like?’ He’s presenting as an asshole. I was really interested in trying to see if I could take the audience from not liking this guy to starting to understand him and then start to actually care about him once the ending happens.”

Mike finds the carefully guarded boundaries of his life quickly eroded beyond his control, many of them even before his close encounter. The couple is on this vacation because they’re trying to get pregnant, and Mike feels everyone is putting the blame for the slow process on him. But what does it say about him if he’s not able to perform or get his wife pregnant as an alpha male should? Meanwhile, Emma doesn’t see the strange things at night that he does … Is he losing his mind? Or, given that she’s a therapist, is she dismissing his reality in order to figure out subtext? As things escalate, their relationship gets squeezed tighter and tighter, and some of the movie’s truest horror is how quickly a relationship can unravel — even if you’re convinced the other person is “the one.”

The film’s heavy lifting would fall apart without the complex performances from its leads. Brittain has the flashier role, a once-dominant male eventually stripped to his core, ceding any control. Pair that emotional heft with some truly gnarly body horror, and it could be a breakout part for the talented actor. Hughes is doing some fascinating work in a diametrically opposite role, one that initially signals a manic pixie put-upon wife, but quickly blooms into darker corners as her desires and secrets are revealed.

“The Crawling” seared itself into my brain and, after a good sleep, it wasn’t just the festival fever that sometimes inspires frenzied praise as a screening lets out. With any luck, horror fans will be able to see this on a big screen and wrap their heads around some of the film’s big questions — many of which I couldn’t touch on here, as not to spoil — and also be thrilled by the alien mayhem.

Watch a teaser trailer for “The Crawling” below.

“The Crawling” is being represented for sales by producer Nick Donadio.

article_text:
News

Meg Onli and Zack Winokur to Curate 2028 Whitney Biennial

Having co-curated the 2024 Biennial, Onli returns to the next edition with Winokur, who founded the American Modern Opera Company.

Meg Onli, an organizer behind some of the Whitney Museum of American Art's signature exhibitions, and Zack Winokur, a performing arts director and co-founder, are the co-curators for the 2028 Whitney Biennial, the museum announced today, November 6.

“Meg is one of the most compelling curatorial voices working today, with an extraordinary ability to champion artists and bring fresh perspectives to the history of American art," Scott Rothkopf, director of the Whitney, said in a statement. "Zack is an equally inventive artistic programmer who has become one of the leading voices of his generation through groundbreaking work across opera, theater, dance, and the visual arts. Their partnership promises a radical new vision for the 2028 Biennial."

The news comes just two months after the 2026 Biennial closed and a month after unionized staff at the museum dodged a full-blown strike ahead of Roy Lichtenstein: Like New , a blockbuster retrospective co-curated by Onli. The Whitney union was one of four New York City museum unions under United Auto Workers 2110 — along with the Brooklyn Museum, the American Folk Art Museum, and the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum — that voted to strike amid drawn-out contract negotiations over low compensation, benefits, and workplace conditions. Hours before the planned strike, unionized staffers ratified their second contract and secured a new wage floor, increased parental and bereavement leave, and stronger safety provisions, among other amendments.

First joining the museum as curator-at-large in 2023, Onli co-curated the 2024 Whitney Biennial , Even Better Than the Real Thing , with Chrissie Iles. That same year, Onli was promoted to Nancy and Fred Poses Curator to lead the Whitney’s painting and sculpture acquisition committee, bringing her previous experience as director and curator of the Underground Museum in Los Angeles and associate curator at the Institute of Contemporary Art at the University of Pennsylvania.

“From the Whitney’s early Annuals to its many subsequent iterations, the Biennial has a rich history of reinvention that is already giving us much to think about," Onli said in a statement. "I couldn’t be more excited to explore what the Biennial can be alongside Zack, who is such a dynamic thinker, and to see where our conversations with artists lead."

Winokur is the co-founder of the American Modern Opera Company, an interdisciplinary collective comprised of 17 singers, musicians, dancers, and other performing artists. He also served as artistic director for Little Island on Pier 55 and NYPopsUp, a statewide initiative aimed at opening performing arts spaces after COVID-19.

“I’m honored to be curating the Whitney Biennial with Meg,” Winokur added in a statement. “Our shared desire to center objects and people and the collision between them already echoes our collaboration. It’s that energy that makes the dialogue with her so fun and inspiring."

Dating back to 1932, the Whitney Biennial remains the longest-running survey of American art, with more than 3,600 artists participating in the exhibition to date. The 83rd edition is slated to open in March 2028.

editorial_title_zh: 铃木望“Looking Through Glass | ガラス越しの眼差”展举办
editorial_excerpt_zh: 东京麹町东条会馆写真研究所将于9月4日起举办铃木望的“Looking Through Glass | 玻璃后的目光”。镜子、窗户、镜头——这些通过光线映照世界的物件，在拓展我们视觉的同时

article_text:
東京の麹町・東條會館写真研究所で9月4日より、鈴木のぞみによる「Looking Through Glass | ガラス越しの眼差し」が開催される。 鏡や窓、レンズ──光を通して世界を映し出すこれらの事物は、私たちの視覚を拡張するとともに、「見ること」と「見られること」を媒介し、人と世界との関係をかたちづくってきた。

本展で鈴木は、19世紀以降の光学機器や写真に着目し、人々の「見る」という経験がどのように形づくられてきたのかを探 究している。眼鏡や望遠鏡、写真制作に用いられてきた道具、そして窓など、人々が世界に眼差しを向けてきたさまざまなガラスに感光剤を塗布し、そこに像を焼き付けることで、眼差しに潜む歴史や記憶を浮かび上がらせる。

会場の東條會館写真研究所は、100年以上にわたり肖像写真を撮影し、人々の人生の節目を記録してきた場所であり、そこには日本の肖像文化とともに、一枚一枚の写真に刻まれた、名もなき個人や家族の記憶が積み重ねられている。「写されること」から始まった日本の写真は、専門的な時代を経て、今や誰でもデータとして残せることが当たり前となった。このように大きな歴史と個人の記憶が交わる場所で、江戸後期に蘭学を通して西洋光学がもたらされてから戦後に至るまで、ガラス越しに世界をとらえてきたさまざまな眼差しを作品を通して体感し、 過去と現在を見つめ直す契機となるだろう。

article_text:
An exhibition dedicated to the music of Ryan Coogler’s Oscar-winning “ Sinners ” has opened at the California African American Museum.

“Sinners: Sounds That Summon” is on view Oct. 20-March 14. Presented in collaboration with Warner Bros. Archives, the presentation is the first museum exhibition devoted to film’s music.

“Sound has the power to form creative worlds that manifest joy, protection, belonging and freedom,” reads an official description of the show. “‘Sinners: Sounds That Summon’ revisits the fan-favorite Club Juke sequence, in which music acts as a portal through time, from traditional African ritual to present-day street dance. Centered around the guitar used by protagonist Sammie ‘Preacher Boy’ Moore, the exhibition brings together costumes, objects and archival material from the film to consider how Black music carries memory, movement, style and spirit across generations.”

Related Stories

Netflix Chiefs Concede That Slowdown in U.S. Viewing Sparked the Content Leadership Shakeup: 'We're Focusing on Execution,' Ted Sarandos Says

“Sinners” follows twin brothers (both played by Michael B. Jordan) in 1932 fighting evil supernatural forces when they return home to the Mississippi Delta. The cast also includes Hailee Steinfeld, Miles Caton, Jack O’Connell, Wunmi Mosaku, Jayme Lawson, Omar Benson Miller, Li Jun Li and Delroy Lindo. The film was nominated for 16 Oscars at the 98th Academy Awards, the most of any film in history. It took home four Oscars: best actor (Jordan), original screenplay (Coogler), cinematography (Autumn Durald Arkapaw) and original score (Ludwig Göransson).

“Sounds That Summon” uses music as the thread that weaves together three themes: Music Makes Sound, Music Makes Movement and Music Makes Worlds. Music Makes Sound looks at instruments through the traditions and histories they carry. Music Makes Movement examines dance as an embodied form of cultural memory, tracing how movement transforms and traverses generations and communities. Music Makes Worlds considers how music extends beyond sound to create language, fashion, identity and community. Alongside Sammie’s guitar, visitors will encounter objects, costumes and props used in the film, including Smoke and Stack’s costumes and the Club Juke sign, evoking the feeling of stepping into the juke joint itself.

The exhibition culminates in Sounds That Carry Us, a participatory experience inspired by the contrast between the joy, safety and collective freedom experienced inside Club Juke and the isolation and danger outside of it. Visitors will be asked to reflect on a song, sound, or genre that carries them back to joy, hope, freedom or community. “Sinners: Sounds That Summon” is co-organized by CAAM and Warner Bros. Archives and curated by Imani Y. Haynes.

editorial_title_zh: 《火焰》50周年：东方是如何被征服的
editorial_excerpt_zh: 解禁：拉梅什·西佩（Ramesh Sippy）于1975年推出的这部惊险刺激的史诗巨作，将西部片、强盗片、无声喜剧和歌舞片的意象杂糅在一起，创造出一部独一无二的邪典经典。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "在柏柏尔语电影《再见卡门》（Adiós Carmen，2013）中，1970年代摩洛哥的一个男孩整天在乡村影院观看印地语歌舞片。其中一场放映的就是拉梅什·西佩的《火焰》。观众们甚至在没有字幕的情况下也被深深吸引，他们对由阿姆贾德·汗（Amjad Khan）饰演的虐待狂反派加巴尔·辛格（Gabbar Singh）发出嘘声，而在舞者海伦（Helen）伴随着粗俗热辣的营地歌舞“Mehbooba Mehbooba”扭动身姿时则发出欢呼。这个场景让我想起了《火焰》自1975年8月上映以来的50年里所经历的传播，特别是在那些印地语电影凭借一首歌所取得的成就远超好莱坞凭借其所有魅力和产业影响力所及的地方。自1950年代以来，印地语电影在俄罗斯、中国、非洲部分地区、加勒比地区和中东都找到了忠实的观众——而作为印度第一部70mm电影的《火焰》也不例外。我能想象出观众在金斯敦跟着哼唱“Yeh Dosti”，在乌兰巴托为赛马达诺（Dhanno）呐喊助威，在汾阳为英雄杰伊（Jai）和韦鲁（Veeru）欢呼，在德黑兰对加巴尔喝倒彩的场景。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "人们普遍认为，《火焰》是有史以来最伟大的印地语通俗电影。在近二十年的时间里，它是该国票房最高的电影；据估计，它仍然保持着售票记录。它在电影院里上映了几个月——在某些情况下甚至长达几年——随后又在电视屏幕上播放了几十年，直到每个人对它都倒背如流。人们经常把《火焰》称为“咖喱西部片”（curry western），但更贴切的称呼或许是“玛萨拉西部片”（masala western）。这个用于混合香料的印地语词汇长期以来一直被用来描述这里所拍摄的这类通俗电影。玛萨拉电影浓郁、风味十足且迎合粗犷的口味，将情节剧、音乐、浪漫、诗歌、喜剧和动作以不断变化的组合交织在一起。从构思之初，《火焰》就被设计成了一部玛萨拉电影，其娱乐规模是前所未见的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "用印地语电影行业的行话来说，一句梗概或电梯游说（elevator pitch）就是“一句话”（one line）。《火焰》在开拍前就已经规模宏大，它拥有四句话。阿努帕玛·乔普拉（Anupama Chopra）在《火焰：一部经典的诞生》（Sholay: The Making of a Classic）一书中写道，编剧二人组萨利姆·汗（Salim Khan）和贾韦德·阿赫塔尔（Javed Akhtar）（合称为“萨利姆-贾韦德”）向导演拉梅什·西佩及其父亲、制片人G·P·西佩（G.P. Sippy）这样推销道：“一个军官的家庭遭到屠杀。他记起了两名曾被军事法庭审判的下属军官。他们是恶棍，但也很勇敢。这位退休军官决定将他们招募进他的复仇使命中。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "值得注意的是，经过长达两年的艰难制作，《火焰》依然忠实于这四句话。其中有一个微调：退休军官变成了一名前功勋警官——塔库尔·巴尔德夫·辛格（Thakur Baldev Singh，桑杰夫·库玛尔饰）。他安排与杰伊（阿米达普·巴强饰）和韦鲁（达曼德拉饰）见面，这两个小偷是他曾经逮捕过的。刚出狱的他们接到了一笔买卖：只要能活捉正在恐吓塔库尔所在的拉姆加尔（Ramgarh）村庄的加巴尔·辛格，就能获得20000卢比，外加50000卢比的官方悬赏。电影的其余部分就在虚构的拉姆加尔展开，这个地方位于印地语腹地的某处，时间大约在60年代末或70年代初。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "西佩父子深知，要卖出一部长达三小时的暴力西部片，他们需要多位明星。他们出面物色了几位，同时也运气不错。达曼德拉和他的准妻子海玛·马利尼（Hema Malini，饰演话多的马车夫巴桑蒂）当时都是超级巨星。桑杰夫·库玛尔同样极受欢迎，而与她的丈夫阿米达普·巴强演对手戏、饰演塔库尔寡居儿媳拉达（Radha）的贾亚·巴杜里（Jaya Bhaduri）则凭《古迪》（Guddi，1971）一炮而红。巴强在签约时还是个身材高瘦、郁郁寡欢且背负一连串票房失利作品的新人，但萨利姆-贾韦德担保了他；而当《火焰》上映时，《永恒的枷锁》（Zanjeer，1973）和《墙》（Deewaar，1975）已经使他成为了该国最具票房号召力的演员。然而，阿姆贾德·汗却是一位不知名的戏剧演员，在电影制作人最初的人选退出后，他在有些惴惴不安的情况下于最后一刻才被选中。影片上映后，他成了所有人津津唯一乐道的话题。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在杰伊和韦鲁抵达拉姆加尔后不久，他们击退了加巴尔帮派歹徒的初次进攻，但在加巴尔亲自领导的更有组织的袭击中，他们几乎寡不敌ئ。在枪战期间，塔库尔表现得异常冷漠，尽管韦鲁拼命呼叫支援，他依然一动不动地站着。“你想知道我为什么不捡起枪吗？”塔库尔后来问韦鲁。萨利姆-贾韦德并没有给出答案，而是把我们带入了一段漫长的倒叙。我们看到年轻时的塔库尔在警察时期逮捕了加巴尔。这名强盗发誓要复仇，不久便越狱并抓获了塔库尔。随后出现了电影中最震撼人心的画面：塔库尔被绑在石柱上，双臂向两侧张开。加巴尔手持双剑在他头顶盘旋，带着威胁的口吻反复说道：“把这两只手给我，塔库尔”（Yeh haath humko de de, Thakur）。随着利落的挥剑动作，画面切回现代，伴随着一阵狂风吹落了塔库尔身上常年披着的披肩，镜头迅速上摇并拉远，显露出他已经失去了双臂。这是一段惊艳的编剧与导演处理，它巧妙地避开了那些绝对无法通过审查委员会的暴力镜头，同时保留了其毁灭性的情感冲击力。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你可以从塞尔吉奥·莱昂内的反派身上看到加巴尔的影子。但实际上，加巴尔在印度电影和西部片经典中都是独树一帜的存在。他是一个令人惊叹的艺术造物，一个擅长辞藻华丽演说的虐待狂：既具吸引力、令人谴责，又无法无天。他就像摇滚巨星般的强盗，随时随地自我赞美，并用第三人称称呼自己：“Gabbar ke taap se tumhe ek hi aadmi bacha sakta hai, ek hi aadmi: khud Gabbar!”（只有一个人能把你从加巴尔的怒火中拯救出来，只有一个人：加巴尔本人！）阿姆贾德·汗那调侃的嗓音榨干了萨利姆-贾韦德那疯狂诗句中的每一滴精髓。当一个心腹苦苦哀求保命、说道“Maine aapka namak khaya hai”（我吃过您的盐）时，加巴尔面无表情地回答说“Ab goli kha”（现在吃铅弹吧），然后开枪打死了他。加巴尔说的每一句话都令人难忘：正因如此，收录了电影台词的特别 LP 唱片才取得了巨大的成功。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "***", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "强盗（源自印地语 daaku，意为匪徒）自默片时代起就是类型片中的脸谱化反派。到了60年代，他们变成了更复杂的形象：受荣誉准则约束的杀手，被爱情或良知软化了的法外狂徒。但直到这十年接近尾声、更硬派的印地语动作片开始崛起时，强盗片才更全面地采用了西部片的视觉风格与态度。这不仅包括引入类型片惯例（独行枪手、高潮迭起的大战），还将塞尔吉奥·莱昂内电影或过去二十年里好莱坞热门影片中的场景原封不动地照搬过来。1973年上映的《Kuchhe "正是在这个四分五裂、玩世不恭的印度，电影《炎热的风》（Sholay）横空出世。这部电影不言而喻、刻意为之是一部西部片，却又不同于以往任何一部西部片。它综合了该类型的三个分支：较黑暗的50年代后好莱坞变体；通心粉西部片；以及融合了音乐情节剧、动作戏和乡村政治的本土“强盗”片。西比的这部史诗片与该类型展开了对话，遵循其规则与母题，同时也引入了令人眼花缭乱的各种色彩、创新、挑衅和意料之外的乐趣。片中有6段歌舞。有被砍断的四肢。有在碎玻璃上的舞蹈。有两段浪漫恋情、两场复仇情节、一场马车追逐、一个为寡妇再婚（在印度长期遭禁）发出的呼吁、一场注定载入史册的劫车行动，以及大量的滑稽闹剧。它在3小时20分钟里浓缩了一生。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "凭借为 vigilante（自警动作片）《Zanjeer》以及讲述兄弟阋墙的戏剧《Deewaar》所创作的剧本——这两部电影都由怒气冲冲的阿米达普·巴强主演——萨利姆-贾韦德将大众印地语电影推向了更硬派、更愤怒的领域。但《炎热的风》则完全是另一回事。所有的幽默和色彩都无法掩盖电影核心处的荒凉。村民们向命运低头；警察无能为力。塔库尔必须失去家庭和双臂，才能意识到通过法律途径复仇是不可能的。贾伊和维鲁是光荣的江洋大盗，他们过上安稳生活、拥有一片土地的梦想最终被暴力和破碎的体制无情摧毁。这种悲观主义呼应了巴强在1970年代所推广的“愤怒青年”银幕形象——这是一个承载着相似屈辱的普通人形象，观众报以了空前狂热的共鸣。", "众所周知，《西部往事》（1968）是一部由其他西部片拼凑而成的西部片。在构思这个故事时，莱昂内、达里奥·阿gento和贝尔纳多·贝托鲁奇设想了一部致敬之作，其中点缀着对数十部经典电影的引用。人们常常错误地将《炎热的风》描述为对莱昂内杰作的翻新，这大概是因为它直接照搬了亨利·方达饰演的弗兰克谋杀定居者家庭的那场戏。在西比的版本中，唯一的区别在于，每当塔库尔的家人被加巴尔枪杀时，画面便会定格，用电影技术的震撼取代了印度审查制度所不允许的银幕暴力。西比还将查尔斯·布朗森角色所吹奏的哀伤口琴曲分配给了贾伊，不过巴强吹奏的曲调更为甜美。", "与莱昂内及其合作者不同，萨利姆-贾韦德对借鉴采取的是实用主义态度而非影迷式的热爱：任何适合他们故事的元素，无论是在西部片、战争片还是默片喜剧中看到，都会被拿来使用，既不抱奢望，也不担心别人会认出出处。西比的电影采用了黑泽明1954年的剑戟片经典《七武士》（或其美国西部片翻版《七侠荡寇志》）的基本结构——尽管除此之外并未多做照搬。这里不是七个人保护一个村庄免受匪徒袭击，而是两个人，尽管推动情节发展的真正动力还是塔库尔的复仇渴望。加巴尔至少部分灵感来源于吉安·玛丽亚·沃隆特在《黄昏双镖客》中饰演的精神病态印第安人，其突发暴力事件总是伴随着咕咕的笑声。热情洋溢的维鲁和沉默寡言的贾伊则让人想起《虎豹小霸王》中两人的关系。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "其中也包含对巴斯特·基顿喜剧杰作《将军号》（1926）在火车袭击戏中的致敬。而那个庸俗的“英属时代”狱警则是喜剧演员阿斯拉尼（Asrani）对《大独裁者》（1940）中查理·卓别林的演绎，甚至连希特勒式的胡子和小地球仪都如出一辙。灵感也来自一些不太知名的电影。《5个人》（The 5-Man Army），一部拥有火车顶部精彩动作戏的1969年意大利西部片，被阿赫塔尔引为灵感来源。在1954年一部名为《罪恶花园》（Garden of Evil）的美国西部片中，理查德·马克德克（Richard Widmark）通过在纸牌上做手脚，诱使加里·库珀（Gary Cooper）和苏珊·海 Hayward（Susan "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "***", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "时间几乎没有动摇《烈火焚城》在印度电影中的核心地位。在对其抽丝剥茧、拆解借鉴了50年之后，导演和编剧们依然能在其中找到可偷师的东西。此后每一个喋喋不休、残忍嗜虐的反派身上都有加巴尔的影子；每一个相爱相杀的主角组合身上都有维鲁和杰伊的痕迹。寻常的印度影迷都能信手拈来地引用一打台词。在印度网络刊物《电影伴侣》（Film Companion）2023年发起的一项民意调查中，由150多名影评人、导演和行业专业人士组成的评审团将《烈火焚城》评为有史以来最伟大的印度电影，排在萨蒂亚吉特·雷伊的《大地之歌》（1955）和古鲁· Dutt 的《痴怨》（1957）之前。像我这样生于80年代的印度人，在看到全片之前大概都是零敲碎打地看过：这有一首歌，那有一个场景，各种碎片散落在文化景观各处。大多数著名的场面——几乎所有涉及加巴尔的场景——我在第一次完整观看时就已经知道了。这或许是印度人在接触正片之前，通过致敬、回忆、恶搞和广告，以表情包（meme）形式体验的第一部电影。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "1975年8月刚上映时，《烈火焚城》的票房开局缓慢；评论褒贬不一，观众也花了数周时间才接受该片的宏大格局与暴力美学。这种不安的开局让许多参与制作的人陷入恐慌。他们差点说服西皮重拍他那阴郁的结局——而这个结局本身为了迎合审查制度就已经被重写和重拍过。在院线公映的版本中，正当塔库尔打算进行宣泄式的复仇时，一个突如其来的警察部队从天而降，打断了他的行动。杰伊死了，拉妲再次失去了依靠，维鲁和巴桑蒂在一起了，却驶向一个未知的未来。留给塔库尔的只有更多的懊悔与内疚。也许加巴尔又一次越狱了。但西皮原本构思的结局要黑暗得多：曾经正直的塔库尔用带钉子的鞋将加巴尔活活踢死。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "今年6月，由电影遗产基金会（Film Heritage Foundation）与谢赫扎德·西皮（Shehzad Sippy，导演的侄子）共同完成的《烈火焚城》全新4K修复版在博洛尼亚的寻影电影节（Il Cinema Ritrovato）上放映。该版本用拉梅什·西皮和编剧们原本设想的结局取代了院线版结局，并加入了两个1975年公映版中没有的被删片段。在一个正规修复片稀少、实体媒介文化不复存在的国家，我对这种（虽说忠于最初构想但仍属）修正主义的剪辑版去取代那段已成为印度历史一部分的版本心存戒惕。话虽如此，我依然无比兴奋能在银幕上看到经过妥当修复的《烈火焚城》。它的许多传奇色彩都围绕着萨利姆-贾韦德和阿姆贾德·汗饰演的加巴尔，以至于连影迷往往也会低估它是一部多么优秀的导演之作。有那么多令人难忘的点睛之笔并非源自剧本或表演：一镜到底的开场戏是如此流畅；村庄环境音的混剪是如此巧妙；杰伊和维鲁为土匪设下陷阱时的动作慢镜头颇有萨姆·佩金帕（Peckinpah）的风范；还有杰伊在一旁凝视并吹着口琴、拉妲在黄昏时分吹熄油灯的动人画面。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在最近的一次重温中，我被杰伊和维鲁伏击土匪之前的一系列镜头迷住了。六名骑马的男子驰骋在地平线上，剪映在血橙色的日出背景下。紧接着是一个向太阳推进的变焦镜头，让芥末黄色占满了整个银幕。这20秒钟是片中绝无仅有的。50年过去了，《烈火焚城》中依然有宝藏藏在显眼处。", "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "In the Berber-language film Adiós Carmen (2013), a boy in 1970s Morocco spends his days watching Hindi musicals at the village cinema. One of the shows is Ramesh Sippy’s Sholay . The audience, riveted even without subtitles, hisses at Gabbar Singh, the sadistic villain played by Amjad Khan, and hoots at dancer Helen as she shimmies through the raunchy campfire number, “Mehbooba Mehbooba.” This scene got me thinking of Sholay ’s travels in the 50 years since its release in August 1975, especially to places where Hindi cinema gets further with a song than Hollywood does with all its glamour and industrial clout. Since the 1950s, Hindi films have found loyal audiences in Russia, China, pockets of Africa, the Caribbean, the Middle East—and Sholay , India’s first 70mm film , was no exception. I can picture viewers singing along to “Yeh Dosti” in Kingston, shouting encouragement to Dhanno the horse in Ulaanbaatar, cheering on heroes Jai and Veeru in Fenyang, jeering at Gabbar in Tehran."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It’s generally accepted that Sholay is the greatest popular Hindi film ever made. It was, for almost two decades, the highest-grossing film in the country; it’s still estimated to hold the record for ticket sales. It played for months in cinemas—even years, in some cases—and then for decades on TV screens, until everyone knew it backwards. Sholay is often called a “curry western,” but a more fitting nomenclature might be “masala western.” The Hindi term for mixed spices has long been used as a descriptor for the kind of popular movies made here. Masala films are strong, flavorful, and suited to robust palates, blending melodrama, music, romance, poetry, comedy, and action in ever-varying combinations. From its inception, Sholay was designed as the masala film , an entertainment on a scale no one had seen before."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In Hindi film -industry parlance, a logline, or elevator pitch, is “one line.” Sholay , expansive before it even started, had four lines. Anupama Chopra writes in Sholay: The Making of a Classic that screenwriting duo Salim Khan and Javed Akhtar (collectively known as “Salim-Javed”) pitched it thus to director Ramesh Sippy and his father, producer G.P. Sippy: “An army officer’s family gets massacred. He remembers two junior officers who had been court-martialed. They are rascals but they are also brave. The retired officer decides to enlist them in his mission for revenge.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Remarkably, through a difficult production that lasted two years, Sholay remained true to these four lines. There was one tweak: the retired army officer became a former police inspector, Thakur Baldev Singh (Sanjeev Kumar). He arranges a meeting with Jai (Amitabh Bachchan) and Veeru (Dharmendra), petty thieves he’d once arrested. Fresh out of jail, they’re made an offer: 20,000 rupees, plus the official reward of 50,000, to bring him Gabbar Singh—who is terrorizing Thakur’s village of Ramgarh—alive. The rest of the film unfolds in the fictional Ramgarh, somewhere in the Hindi heartland, sometime in the late ’60s or early ’70s."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The Sippys knew they needed multiple stars to sell a violent three-hour western. They went out and got some, and also got lucky. Dharmendra and his wife-to-be, Hema Malini, who plays chatty tonga driver Basanti, were massive stars. Sanjeev Kumar was extremely popular as well, and Jaya Bhaduri—cast opposite her husband, Amitabh Bachchan, as Thakur’s widowed daughter-in-law, Radha—had had a hit with Guddi (1971). Bachchan was a lanky brooder with a string of flops when he signed, but Salim-Javed vouched for him, and by the time Sholay was released, Zanjeer (1973) and Deewaar (1975) had made him the biggest box-office draw in the country. Amjad Khan, however, was an unknown theater actor, cast at the last moment and with some trepidation after the filmmakers’ first choice withdrew. Once the film opened, he was all anyone could talk about."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Soon after Jai and Veeru’s arrival in Ramgarh, they repel an initial advance by Gabbar’s gang of outlaws, but are nearly outgunned in a more organized attack led by Gabbar himself. Thakur is strangely inert during the shootout, standing motionless despite Veeru’s frantic calls for assistance. “Do you want to know why I didn’t pick up the gun?” Thakur asks Veeru later. Instead of offering an answer, Salim-Javed send us into a long flashback. We see a younger Thakur, in his police-force days, arrest Gabbar. The dacoit swears revenge, soon breaks out of jail, and captures Thakur. Then comes the film ’s most electrifying image: Thakur tied to stone columns, arms outstretched on either side. Gabbar looms over him, a sword in each hand, repeating menacingly, “ Yeh haath humko de de , Thakur” (Give me these arms, Thakur). As the swords swish down, there’s a cut to the present day, and a quick pan up and zoom out as a gust of wind blows off Thakur’s ever-present shawl, revealing that he has no arms. It’s a stunning bit of writing and direction, skirting a moment of violence that would never have made it past the censor board, but retaining its emotional devastation."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "You can draw a line from Sergio Leone’s villains to Gabbar. But really, Gabbar stands alone, in Indian cinema and the western movie canon. He’s an astonishing creation, a sadist with a gift for ornate speechifying: magnetic, reprehensible, and uncontrollable. He’s the bandit as rock star, self-eulogizing on the fly, referring to himself in the third person: “Gabbar ke taap se tumhe ek hi aadmi bacha sakta hai, ek hi aadmi: khud Gabbar!” (Only one man can save you from Gabbar’s wrath: Gabbar himself!) Amjad Khan’s teasing voice extracts every bit of juice from Salim-Javed’s unhinged poetry. When a henchman begs for his life, saying “ Maine aapka namak khaya hai ” (I’ve eaten your salt), Gabbar deadpans, “ Ab goli kha ” (Now eat lead), and shoots him. Everything Gabbar says is memorable: he’s the reason a special LP featuring the film ’s dialogue became a massive success."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "***"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The dacoit (from the Hindi daaku , or bandit) had been a stock villain since the silent era. In the ’60s, they became more complex figures: killers bound by honor codes, outlaws softened by love or conscience. But it was only when a tougher Hindi action cinema began to take hold by the decade’s end that dacoit films more fully adopted the look and attitude of westerns. This ranged from incorporating genre tropes (the lone gunslinger, the climactic pitched battle) to lifting scenes wholesale from Sergio Leone films or Hollywood hits from the previous two decades. The freeze-frame ending of Kuchhe Dhaage (1973) recalls Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid (1969), while the boisterous Khote Sikkay (1974) is essentially The Magnificent Seven (1960) crossed with For a Few Dollars More (1965) and a soundtrack of barely altered Morricone hits."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Even as Hindi cinema seemed to be building up to a great western in the ’70s, India was breaking down. The first generation of independent Indians was growing restless. The dreams of newly won freedom had faded. Unemployment was rising. There were student protests, and strikes. Prime Minister Indira Gandhi saw her popularity plummet, and in June of 1975, she announced a state of nationwide emergency. Civil liberties were suspended and severe restrictions placed on the press and political opposition. It was lifted two years later."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It was into this fractured, cynical India that Sholay emerged. The film is self-evidently, intentionally, a western, yet it’s unlike any other western ever made. It synthesizes three strands of the genre: the darker, post-’50s Hollywood variant; the spaghetti western; and the homegrown “dacoit” film , which combined musical melodrama with action and rural politics. Sippy’s epic is in conversation with the genre, working with its rules and motifs, but it also introduces a dazzling array of shadings, innovations, provocations, and stray delights. There are six musical numbers. There are severed limbs. There’s dancing on broken glass. There are two romances, two revenge plots, a horse-carriage chase, a plea for widow remarriage (long verboten in India), a train hijacking for the ages, and a ton of slapstick. It’s a lifetime in three hours and 20 minutes."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "With their scripts for the vigilante action film Zanjeer and the warring-brothers drama Deewaar , both of which starred a seething Amitabh Bachchan, Salim-Javed had pushed popular Hindi cinema into tougher, angrier territory. But Sholay was something else. All the humor and color can’t hide the bleakness at the film ’s core. The villagers are resigned to their fate; the police are powerless. Thakur must lose his family and his arms to realize the impossibility of lawful revenge. Jai and Veeru are honourable thieves whose dreams of settling down with a plot of land are undone by violence and a broken system. This pessimism echoed the “angry young man” persona Bachchan was popularizing in the 1970s—an everyman figure that audiences, burdened with similar indignities, responded to with unprecedented fervor."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "***"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Once Upon a Time in the West (1968) was, famously, a western stitched from other westerns. In crafting the story, Leone, Dario Argento, and Bernardo Bertolucci envisioned an homage, studded with references to dozens of classic films . Sholay is often described, erroneously, as a reworking of Leone’s opus, probably because of its straight lift of the scene in which Henry Fonda’s Frank murders a settler family. The only difference in Sippy’s version of this scene is that each time a member of Thakur’s family is shot by Gabbar, the frame freezes, the jolt of film technique replacing the on-screen violence Indian censors wouldn’t allow. Sippy also assigns the plaintive harmonica played by Charles Bronson’s character to Jai, though Bachchan plays a sweeter tune."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Unlike Leone and his collaborators, Salim-Javed had a practical, rather than cinephilic, approach to borrowing: anything that fit their story, whether they saw it in a western or war film or silent comedy, would be used, with neither expectation nor worry that someone would recognize the source. Sippy’s film takes its basic structure—though not much else—from Akira Kurosawa’s 1954 chanbara classic Seven Samurai (or its American western remake, The Magnificent Seven ). article_text:
In the Berber-language film Adiós Carmen (2013), a boy in 1970s Morocco spends his days watching Hindi musicals at the village cinema. One of the shows is Ramesh Sippy’s Sholay . The audience, riveted even without subtitles, hisses at Gabbar Singh, the sadistic villain played by Amjad Khan, and hoots at dancer Helen as she shimmies through the raunchy campfire number, “Mehbooba Mehbooba.” This scene got me thinking of Sholay ’s travels in the 50 years since its release in August 1975, especially to places where Hindi cinema gets further with a song than Hollywood does with all its glamour and industrial clout. Since the 1950s, Hindi films have found loyal audiences in Russia, China, pockets of Africa, the Caribbean, the Middle East—and Sholay , India’s first 70mm film , was no exception. I can picture viewers singing along to “Yeh Dosti” in Kingston, shouting encouragement to Dhanno the horse in Ulaanbaatar, cheering on heroes Jai and Veeru in Fenyang, jeering at Gabbar in Tehran.

It’s generally accepted that Sholay is the greatest popular Hindi film ever made. It was, for almost two decades, the highest-grossing film in the country; it’s still estimated to hold the record for ticket sales. It played for months in cinemas—even years, in some cases—and then for decades on TV screens, until everyone knew it backwards. Sholay is often called a “curry western,” but a more fitting nomenclature might be “masala western.” The Hindi term for mixed spices has long been used as a descriptor for the kind of popular movies made here. Masala films are strong, flavorful, and suited to robust palates, blending melodrama, music, romance, poetry, comedy, and action in ever-varying combinations. From its inception, Sholay was designed as the masala film , an entertainment on a scale no one had seen before.

In Hindi film -industry parlance, a logline, or elevator pitch, is “one line.” Sholay , expansive before it even started, had four lines. Anupama Chopra writes in Sholay: The Making of a Classic that screenwriting duo Salim Khan and Javed Akhtar (collectively known as “Salim-Javed”) pitched it thus to director Ramesh Sippy and his father, producer G.P. Sippy: “An army officer’s family gets massacred. He remembers two junior officers who had been court-martialed. They are rascals but they are also brave. The retired officer decides to enlist them in his mission for revenge.”

Remarkably, through a difficult production that lasted two years, Sholay remained true to these four lines. There was one tweak: the retired army officer became a former police inspector, Thakur Baldev Singh (Sanjeev Kumar). He arranges a meeting with Jai (Amitabh Bachchan) and Veeru (Dharmendra), petty thieves he’d once arrested. Fresh out of jail, they’re made an offer: 20,000 rupees, plus the official reward of 50,000, to bring him Gabbar Singh—who is terrorizing Thakur’s village of Ramgarh—alive. The rest of the film unfolds in the fictional Ramgarh, somewhere in the Hindi heartland, sometime in the late ’60s or early ’70s.

The Sippys knew they needed multiple stars to sell a violent three-hour western. They went out and got some, and also got lucky. Dharmendra and his wife-to-be, Hema Malini, who plays chatty tonga driver Basanti, were massive stars. Sanjeev Kumar was extremely popular as well, and Jaya Bhaduri—cast opposite her husband, Amitabh Bachchan, as Thakur’s widowed daughter-in-law, Radha—had had a hit with Guddi (1971). Bachchan was a lanky brooder with a string of flops when he signed, but Salim-Javed vouched for him, and by the time Sholay was released, Zanjeer (1973) and Deewaar (1975) had made him the biggest box-office draw in the country. Amjad Khan, however, was an unknown theater actor, cast at the last moment and with some trepidation after the filmmakers’ first choice withdrew. Once the film opened, he was all anyone could talk about.

Soon after Jai and Veeru’s arrival in Ramgarh, they repel an initial advance by Gabbar’s gang of outlaws, but are nearly outgunned in a more organized attack led by Gabbar himself. Thakur is strangely inert during the shootout, standing motionless despite Veeru’s frantic calls for assistance. “Do you want to know why I didn’t pick up the gun?” Thakur asks Veeru later. Instead of offering an answer, Salim-Javed send us into a long flashback. We see a younger Thakur, in his police-force days, arrest Gabbar. The dacoit swears revenge, soon breaks out of jail, and captures Thakur. Then comes the film ’s most electrifying image: Thakur tied to stone columns, arms outstretched on either side. Gabbar looms over him, a sword in each hand, repeating menacingly, “ Yeh haath humko de de , Thakur” (Give me these arms, Thakur). As the swords swish down, there’s a cut to the present day, and a quick pan up and zoom out as a gust of wind blows off Thakur’s ever-present shawl, revealing that he has no arms. It’s a stunning bit of writing and direction, skirting a moment of violence that would never have made it past the censor board, but retaining its emotional devastation.

You can draw a line from Sergio Leone’s villains to Gabbar. But really, Gabbar stands alone, in Indian cinema and the western movie canon. He’s an astonishing creation, a sadist with a gift for ornate speechifying: magnetic, reprehensible, and uncontrollable. He’s the bandit as rock star, self-eulogizing on the fly, referring to himself in the third person: “Gabbar ke taap se tumhe ek hi aadmi bacha sakta hai, ek hi aadmi: khud Gabbar!” (Only one man can save you from Gabbar’s wrath: Gabbar himself!) Amjad Khan’s teasing voice extracts every bit of juice from Salim-Javed’s unhinged poetry. When a henchman begs for his life, saying “ Maine aapka namak khaya hai ” (I’ve eaten your salt), Gabbar deadpans, “ Ab goli kha ” (Now eat lead), and shoots him. Everything Gabbar says is memorable: he’s the reason a special LP featuring the film ’s dialogue became a massive success.

***

The dacoit (from the Hindi daaku , or bandit) had been a stock villain since the silent era. In the ’60s, they became more complex figures: killers bound by honor codes, outlaws softened by love or conscience. But it was only when a tougher Hindi action cinema began to take hold by the decade’s end that dacoit films more fully adopted the look and attitude of westerns. This ranged from incorporating genre tropes (the lone gunslinger, the climactic pitched battle) to lifting scenes wholesale from Sergio Leone films or Hollywood hits from the previous two decades. The freeze-frame ending of Kuchhe Dhaage (1973) recalls Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid (1969), while the boisterous Khote Sikkay (1974) is essentially The Magnificent Seven (1960) crossed with For a Few Dollars More (1965) and a soundtrack of barely altered Morricone hits.

Even as Hindi cinema seemed to be building up to a great western in the ’70s, India was breaking down. The first generation of independent Indians was growing restless. The dreams of newly won freedom had faded. Unemployment was rising. There were student protests, and strikes. Prime Minister Indira Gandhi saw her popularity plummet, and in June of 1975, she announced a state of nationwide emergency. Civil liberties were suspended and severe restrictions placed on the press and political opposition. It was lifted two years later.

It was into this fractured, cynical India that Sholay emerged. The film is self-evidently, intentionally, a western, yet it’s unlike any other western ever made. It synthesizes three strands of the genre: the darker, post-’50s Hollywood variant; the spaghetti western; and the homegrown “dacoit” film , which combined musical melodrama with action and rural politics. Sippy’s epic is in conversation with the genre, working with its rules and motifs, but it also introduces a dazzling array of shadings, innovations, provocations, and stray delights. There are six musical numbers. There are severed limbs. There’s dancing on broken glass. There are two romances, two revenge plots, a horse-carriage chase, a plea for widow remarriage (long verboten in India), a train hijacking for the ages, and a ton of slapstick. It’s a lifetime in three hours and 20 minutes.

With their scripts for the vigilante action film Zanjeer and the warring-brothers drama Deewaar , both of which starred a seething Amitabh Bachchan, Salim-Javed had pushed popular Hindi cinema into tougher, angrier territory. But Sholay was something else. All the humor and color can’t hide the bleakness at the film ’s core. The villagers are resigned to their fate; the police are powerless. Thakur must lose his family and his arms to realize the impossibility of lawful revenge. Jai and Veeru are honourable thieves whose dreams of settling down with a plot of land are undone by violence and a broken system. This pessimism echoed the “angry young man” persona Bachchan was popularizing in the 1970s—an everyman figure that audiences, burdened with similar indignities, responded to with unprecedented fervor.

***

Once Upon a Time in the West (1968) was, famously, a western stitched from other westerns. In crafting the story, Leone, Dario Argento, and Bernardo Bertolucci envisioned an homage, studded with references to dozens of classic films . Sholay is often described, erroneously, as a reworking of Leone’s opus, probably because of its straight lift of the scene in which Henry Fonda’s Frank murders a settler family. The only difference in Sippy’s version of this scene is that each time a member of Thakur’s family is shot by Gabbar, the frame freezes, the jolt of film technique replacing the on-screen violence Indian censors wouldn’t allow. Sippy also assigns the plaintive harmonica played by Charles Bronson’s character to Jai, though Bachchan plays a sweeter tune.

Unlike Leone and his collaborators, Salim-Javed had a practical, rather than cinephilic, approach to borrowing: anything that fit their story, whether they saw it in a western or war film or silent comedy, would be used, with neither expectation nor worry that someone would recognize the source. Sippy’s film takes its basic structure—though not much else—from Akira Kurosawa’s 1954 chanbara classic Seven Samurai (or its American western remake, The Magnificent Seven ). Instead of seven men protecting a village from bandits, here there are two, though the driving force is really Thakur’s desire for vengeance. Gabbar is at least partly inspired by Gian Maria Volonté’s psychotic Indio in For a Few Dollars More , with his gurgling laugh punctuating sudden acts of violence. Ebullient Veeru and reserved Jai recall the relationship between Butch Cassidy and Sundance.

There’s also a nod to Buster Keaton’s comic masterpiece The General (1926) during the train attack. And the buffoonish, “British-era” jailer is comedian Asrani’s take on Charlie Chaplin in The Great Dictator (1940), down to his Hitler moustache and globe. Ideas came from lesser-known films too. The 5-Man Army , a 1969 spaghetti western with a terrific action sequence on top of a train, was cited by Akhtar as an inspiration. In a 1954 American western called Garden of Evil , Richard Widmark gets Gary Cooper to leave a potentially fatal shootout along with Susan Hayward by tricking him at cards. This scene is echoed in Sholay , when Jai flips his silver rupee coin to decide who’ll hold off the dacoits at the bridge and who’ll rush to the village with Basanti to pick up ammunition (Veeru never suspects that it’s a two-headed coin). It’s a typically deft lift by Salim-Javed: recognizing the potential in a stray scene, filing it away, and finding the perfect fit for it decades later. That Sholay ended up a tapestry of global cinema influences is one of its incidental pleasures. Sippy and Salim-Javed were concerned only with getting the right blend of masala.

***

Time has done little to disturb Sholay ’s centrality in Indian cinema. After 50 years of stripping it for parts, directors and writers still find things to steal. Every talky, sadistic villain in its wake has a bit of Gabbar in him; every sweet-sour lead duo has some of Veeru and Jai. The average Indian moviegoer can easily quote a dozen of its lines on command. In a poll conducted by the Indian web publication Film Companion in 2023, a pool of over 150 critics, directors, and industry professionals voted Sholay the best Indian film of all time, ahead of Satyajit Ray’s Pather Panchali (1955) and Guru Dutt’s Pyaasa (1957). Indians of my generation, born in the ’80s, likely saw it piecemeal before they saw it whole: a song here, a scene there, fragments scattered across the cultural landscape. Most of the famous scenes—nearly all the ones involving Gabbar—I already knew when I watched it for the first time. This might have been the first film Indians experienced in meme form before the real thing, through homages, reminiscences, parodies, advertisements.

Back in August 1975, Sholay got off to a slow start at the box office; reviews were mixed and audiences took a couple of weeks to come to grips with the film ’s scale and violence. This uneasy start caused many involved with the production to panic. They almost convinced Sippy to reshoot his downbeat ending—which itself was rewritten and reshot to accommodate the censors. In the theatrical-release version, just as Thakur looks to take cathartic revenge, a deus-ex-machina police troop appears and cuts him short. Jai is dead, Radha is bereft once again, Veeru and Basanti are together but headed into an uncertain future. Thakur is left with even more regret and guilt. Maybe Gabbar breaks out of jail again. But Sippy’s intended ending was bleaker still: the once-upstanding Thakur kicks Gabbar to death with spiked shoes.

In June, a new 4K restoration of Sholay by the Film Heritage Foundation and Shehzad Sippy (the director’s nephew) played at Il Cinema Ritrovato in Bologna. It replaces the theatrical-release ending with the one Ramesh Sippy and the writers intended, and includes two deleted scenes that weren’t in the 1975 cut. In a country where proper restorations are rare and physical-media culture is nonexistent, I’m wary of a revisionist cut (albeit one that honors the original vision) supplanting the version that became a part of India’s history. That said, I couldn’t be more excited to see Sholay , properly restored, on the big screen. So much of its legend centers on Salim-Javed and Amjad Khan’s Gabbar that even fans tend to underestimate what a well-directed film it is. There are so many memorable flourishes that don’t stem from writing or performance: the smoothness of the one-shot opening scene; the deft montage of ambient village sounds; the Peckinpah-like slow-motion action when Jai and Veeru lay a trap for the bandits; the haunting image of Radha extinguishing the lamps at dusk as Jai looks on and plays harmonica.

In a recent viewing, I was captivated by a series of shots preceding Jai and Veeru’s ambush of the dacoits. Six men on horseback gallop across the horizon, silhouetted against a blood-orange sunrise. This is followed by a zoom into the sun, filling the entire screen with mustard yellow. These 20 seconds are unlike anything else in the film . Fifty years of Sholay and still there are treasures hiding in plain sight.

article_text:
When we want to talk about nature, do we have to go to Antarctica or the Amazon rainforest to make a well-founded point?

Alongside the essential news on a world that is disappearing or on the verge of doing so, isn’t legitimate to take an interest in the world that is adapting?

For my part, I believe that daily observation, as the seasons, years and decades pass, allows us to show the reality of nature over the vast majority of the planet: one in which humans and the land influence one another.

I’d like to present a series, month by month, featuring two images per month, taken over the years.

Nothing spectacular or exceptional, just a shared living space comprising wasteland, pine forests and plateaus, farmland and vineyards. Simple images, places of unadorned beauty, diverse vegetation that changes with the seasons, and the passage of time and climate change evident throughout these years of photography – this is what I propose.

I have chosen the square black and white format to emphasise the timeless nature of these images.

translated_excerpt_zh: 当我们想谈论大自然时,我们是否必须去南极洲或亚马逊雨林,以便做出一个有基础的点? 旁边的这篇文章是Henri Kartmann - Chronicles of Haute-Provence est apparu en premier on The Eye of Photography Magazine。

title_original: Chris Rock, Quinta Brunson, Jaafar Jackson, Chiwetel Ejiofor Among Honorees For 9th Critics Choice Celebration Of Black Cinema & TV
editorial_title_zh: 克里斯·洛克、昆塔·布伦森、杰法·杰克逊、切瓦特·埃加福特等将获得第九届评论家选择黑人电影与电视庆典表彰
editorial_excerpt_zh: 评论家选择协会第九届年度黑人电影与电视庆典迎来了全明星阵容。黛比·艾伦、克里斯·洛克、昆塔·布伦森、杰法·杰克逊和切瓦特·埃加福特将成为今年活动的获奖者之一，活动将于11月16日举行……

"“我们很自豪地宣布，庆祝活动仍在继续，”评论家选择协会黑人电影与电视庆典执行制片人兼编剧肖恩·爱德华兹（Shawn Edwards）表示，“在黑人文化和黑人历史遭受直接攻击的时刻，评论家选择协会坚决致力于表彰黑人电影和电视领域的杰出成果。这不是我们不得不做的事，而是我们发自内心想做的事。为这些勇敢且富有远见的叙事者创造一个共聚一堂并接受表彰的夜晚，既是我们的荣幸，也是我们每年坚定不移去践行的承诺。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://deadline.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/CBCTV2026-LOGO.png?w=300", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Deadline · Film", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "据 CCA 透露，今年黑人电影与电视庆典的获奖者将包括：", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "在 Deadline 上观看", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "作为学院荣誉奖得主、六次艾美奖得主和两次托尼奖提名者，黛比·艾伦将荣获偶像奖，以表彰她近五年来非凡的职业生涯以及跨越近五十年的持久文化影响力，她拥有超过140个表演、制片和导演署名。致敬环节将庆祝《不同世界》（A Different World）及其2026年网飞（Netflix）续集的传奇色彩，将黑人大学经历带给新一代。艾伦担任了原版剧集的制片人，并执导了其144集中的83集，帮助塑造了一部探讨艾滋病毒、肤色歧视和种族主义的开创性剧集。她回归担任续集的执行制片人兼导演，并再次饰演朗霍恩医生。该剧已获续订第二季。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "两届艾美奖得主、评论家选择奖得主昆塔·布伦森（Quinta Brunson）将荣获开拓者奖（Groundbreaker Award），以表彰她为ABC电视台热播剧《小学风云》（Abbott Elementary）所做出的创作、执行制片及主演贡献，该剧于10月7日迎来了第六季的首播。这部由华纳兄弟电视公司和20世纪电视公司联合制作的热门喜剧迄今已获得37项艾美奖提名。布伦森在2022年创造了艾美奖历史，成为第一位获得喜剧编剧奖的黑人女性单人得主；而在2024年，她又成为了40多年来第一位荣获喜剧类剧集最佳女主角的黑人女演员。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "奥斯卡奖和评论家选择奖提名者切瓦特·埃加福特将凭借其在 A24 心理恐怖片《后室》（Backrooms）中的表现荣获先锋奖。该片由凯恩·帕森斯（Kane Parsons）执导，这部恐怖热片在本土斩获8140万美元票房，打破了 A24 首周末上映票房的历史纪录，成为其迄今为止票房最高的电影，全球票房超过4亿美元。埃加福特与雷娜特·赖因斯韦（Renate Reinsve）共同领衔主演这部改编自帕森斯病毒式 YouTube 系列视频的作品。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "艾美奖和格莱美奖得主克里斯·洛克将凭借 A24 的《Misty Green》荣获导演奖。该片是洛克作为导演的第四部叙事长片。他同时担任该片的编剧、制片人和联合主演，片中罗莎琳·埃莱扎尔（Rosalind Eleazar，《流人》）奉献了其演艺生涯的决定性表演，饰演一位为复兴演艺事业而战的女演员。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "艾美奖得主拉莫恩·莫里斯将凭借在 Prime Video 超级英雄剧集《蜘蛛侠：暗影》（Spider-Noir）中饰演罗比·罗伯逊（Robbie Robertson）的表现荣获喜剧奖。该剧赢得了11项艾美奖提名，并斩获5项艾美奖。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "普利策奖得主卡托里·霍尔（Katori Hall）将凭借 Starz 电视台的《权欲第二篇章：力量》（P-Valley）荣获剧集运作人奖。该剧将于12月4日携双集首播回归第三季也是最终季。霍尔根据自己的同名戏剧创作了该剧，并执导了两集首播。《P-Valley》是 Starz 表现最好的现行原创剧集，第二季的多平台平均观众数达到1160万。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "杰法·杰克逊将凭借在狮门影业传记片《迈克尔》（Michael）中备受好评、备受大众喜爱的迈克尔·杰克逊扮演获得电影类演员奖，这也是他的银幕处女作。该片不仅创下了音乐传记片的纪录——成为有史以来第一部全球票房超过10亿美元的各类传记片，也是狮门影业历史上最成功的发行作品。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "艾美奖提名者安东尼·麦凯将凭借其在 Apple TV 即将推出的八集盗窃剧《12 12 12》中的工作荣获剧集类演员奖，他也担任该剧的执行制片人。麦凯在剧中饰演一名名誉扫地的 FBI 特工，与杰米·多南（Jamie Dornan）饰演的职业罪犯在欧洲展开猫鼠游戏。《12 12 12》将于11月13日在 Apple TV 全球首播。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "艾美奖提名者斯蒂芬·詹姆斯将凭借在亚马逊米高梅影业（Amazon MGM Studios）《我演洛奇》（I Play Rocky）中对卡尔·韦瑟斯（Carl Weathers）的刻画荣获电影类最佳男配角奖。该片由奥斯卡奖得主彼得·法雷里（Peter Farrelly）执导，记录了原版《洛奇》的幕后制作历程，以及西尔维斯特·史泰龙坚持撰写剧本并亲自主演的坚定信念。这部传记剧情片将于11月上映。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "托尼奖得主、奥斯卡奖和艾美奖提名者苏菲·奥康多（Sophie Okonedo）将凭借其在独立电影公司（Independent Film Company）出品、凯利·奥沙利文（Kelly O'Sullivan）与亚历克斯·汤普森（Alex Thompson）执导的成长题材剧情片《Mouse》中的表演，荣获电影类最佳女配角奖。该片在柏林电影节上首映，并将于下个月开始在各大院线公映。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "美国演员工会奖（SAG Award）及评论家选择奖提名者阿托·艾桑多（Ato Essandoh）将凭借其在Netflix剧情剧集《外交官》（The Diplomat）中饰演斯图尔特·海福德（Stuart Hayford）的表现，荣获剧集类最佳男配角奖。这部政治惊悚剧在2025年和2026年两度获得艾美奖最佳剧情剧集提名，并于10月15日迎来了第四季的回归。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "托尼奖提名者昆西·泰勒·伯恩斯坦（Quincy Tyler Bernstine）将凭借其在Hulu惊悚剧《Furious》中饰演诺拉·华盛顿（Nora Washington）的表现，荣获剧集类最佳女配角奖。该剧由伊丽莎白·梅里韦瑟（Elizabeth Meriwether）创作，讲述了一名联邦调查局特工追捕一名精于算计的女性连环杀手的故事。伯恩斯坦抓人眼球的表演已成为2026年备受瞩目的新剧之一中的一大亮点。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "此外，Starz电视网还将为伯恩斯坦的奖项授予特殊的Starz #TakeTheLead称号，作为其持续致力于扩大由女性、关于女性、为女性以及由代表性不足的观众创作并面向他们的叙事作品承诺的一部分。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "新锐电影人阿里·埃西里（Arie Esiri）和楚科·埃西里（Chuko Esiri）将凭借霓虹娱乐（Neon）出品的《Clarissa》荣获突破导演奖，该片是尼日利亚当代拉各斯背景下对弗吉尼亚·伍尔夫（Virginia Woolf）小说《达洛维夫人》（Mrs. Dalloway）的重新演绎。该片由黑人电影与电视庆典的另一位获奖者奥康多与大卫·奥伊罗（David Oyelowo）、阿yo·埃德比利（Ayo Edebiri）、印度·阿马蒂菲奥（India Amarteifio）和托希布·吉莫（Toheeb Jimoh）共同主演。该片在2026年戛纳电影节的“导演双周”单元首映，成为该电影节历史上仅有的第二部入选的尼日利亚故事片，并于12月11日在部分影院上映。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "贾伦·贝斯特（Jaalen Best）将凭借在Prime Video的穆罕默德·阿里传记剧集《The Greatest》中饰演卡修斯·克莱（Cassius Clay）的出色表现，荣获新星奖（Rising Star Award）。这是首部获得授权、关于阿里生平的剧集，其执行制片人包括阿里的遗孀朗尼·阿里（Lonnie Ali）以及乔什·瓦克利（Josh Wakely）和迈克尔·B·乔丹（Michael B. Jordan）。该剧将于11月4日在Prime Video首播。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "评论家选择协会的黑人电影与电视庆典将由Hammond Infante Productions的马德琳·哈蒙德（Madelyn Hammond）、哈维尔·因芬特（Javier Infante）和埃拉·卡尔森（Ella Carlson）共同制作。", "translated": true}]

Henson Encourages Artists To ‘Knock Down’ Walls, Sarah Finn Celebrates Casting Community & More At 2026 Newport Beach Film Festival Honors", "links": [{"text": "Taraji P. Henson Encourages Artists To ‘Knock Down’ Walls, Sarah Finn Celebrates Casting Community & More At 2026 Newport Beach Film Festival Honors", "url": "https://deadline.com/2026/10/newport-beach-film-festival-2026-honors-brunch-1237170107/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“We are proud to announce that the celebration continues,” said Shawn Edwards, executive producer and writer of the Critics Choice Association’s Celebration of Black Cinema & Television. “At a time when there has been a direct assault on Black culture and Black history, the Critics Choice Association stands firmly committed to recognizing the best in Black cinema and television. This isn’t something that we have to do, it’s something that we want to do. Creating a space where these bold and visionary storytellers can come together for an evening and be honored is our privilege and something that we are firmly committed to doing each year.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://deadline.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/CBCTV2026-LOGO.png?w=300", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Deadline · Film"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Honorees for this year’s Celebration of Black Cinema & Television will include, per the CCA:"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Watch on Deadline"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Academy Honorary Award recipient, six-time Emmy winner, and two-time Tony nominee Debbie Allen will receive the Icon Award, recognizing her extraordinary career and enduring cultural impact across nearly five decades, with more than 140 acting, producing, and directing credits. Her tribute will celebrate the legacy of A Different World and its 2026 Netflix sequel, bringing the Black college experience to a new generation. Allen produced the original series and directed 83 of its 144 episodes, helping shape a groundbreaking show that addressed HIV, colorism, and racism. She returns as executive producer and director of the sequel and reprises her role as Dr. Langhorne. The series has already been renewed for a second season."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Two-time Emmy Award winner and Critics Choice Award winner Quinta Brunson will receive the Groundbreaker Award for creating, executive producing, and starring in ABC’s Abbott Elementary , which premiered its sixth season on Oct. 7. Produced by Warner Bros. Television & 20th Television, the hit comedy has earned 37 Emmy nominations to date. Brunson made Emmy history in 2022 as the first solo Black woman to win for comedy writing, and in 2024 she became the first Black actress in more than 40 years to win Outstanding Lead Actress in a Comedy Series."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Academy Award and Critics Choice Award nominee Chiwetel Ejiofor will receive the Vanguard Award for his work in A24’s psychological horror film Backrooms . Directed by Kane Parsons, the horror hit opened to $81.4 million domestically, shattering the previous record for an A24 opening weekend release and becoming its highest-grossing film to date, earning more than $400 million worldwide. Ejiofor leads the cast alongside Renate Reinsve in the adaptation of Parsons’ viral YouTube series."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Emmy and Grammy Award winner Chris Rock will receive the Director Award for A24’s Misty Green . The film marks Rock’s fourth narrative feature as a director. He also wrote, produced, and co-stars in the film, which stars Rosalind Eleazar ( Slow Horses) in a career-defining turn portraying an actress fighting to revive her career."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Emmy Award winner Lamorne Morris will receive the Comedy Award for his work as Robbie Robertson in Prime Video’s superhero series Spider-Noir. The series earned 11 Emmy nominations, and won five Emmy Awards."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Pulitzer Prize winner Katori Hall will be honored with the Showrunner Award for Starz’s P-Valley . The series returns December 4 for its third and final season with a two-episode premiere. Hall created the series from her own play and directed both premiere episodes. P-Valley is Starz’s best-performing current original, with Season 2 averaging 11.6 million multiplatform viewers."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Jaafar Jackson will receive the Actor Award – Film for his critically acclaimed, crowd-pleasing portrayal of Michael Jackson in Lionsgate’s biographical film Michael , which marks his acting debut. The film set records not only for a music biopic—it became the first biopic of any kind to gross more than $1 billion worldwide and is the most successful release in Lionsgate history."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Emmy Award nominee Anthony Mackie will be honored with the Actor Award – Series for his work in Apple TV’s upcoming 12 12 12 , which he also executive produces. Mackie plays a disgraced FBI agent locked in a cat-and-mouse game across Europe with Jamie Dornan’s career criminal, in the eight-episode heist drama. 12 12 12 premieres globally on Apple TV on Nov. 13."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Emmy nominee Stephan James will be honored with the Supporting Actor Award – Film for his portrayal of Carl Weathers in Amazon MGM Studios’ I Play Rocky . Directed by Academy Award winner Peter Farrelly, the film chronicles the making of the original Rocky and Sylvester Stallone’s determination to write and star in it. The biographical drama opens in November."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Tony Award winner and Academy Award and Emmy nominee Sophie Okonedo will receive the Supporting Actress Award – Film for her performance in Independent Film Company’s coming-of-age drama Mouse , directed by Kelly O’Sullivan and Alex Thompson. The drama premiered at the Berlin Film Festival and begins its theatrical engagements next month."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "SAG Award and Critics Choice Award nominee Ato Essandoh will receive the Supporting Actor Award – Series for his work as Stuart Hayford in Netflix’s drama series The Diplomat. The political thriller was nominated for Outstanding Drama Series at the Emmys in 2025 and again in 2026, and returned for its fourth season October 15."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Tony Award nominee Quincy Tyler Bernstine will receive the Supporting Actress Award – Series for her work as Nora Washington in Hulu’s Furious . Created by Elizabeth Meriwether, the thriller follows an FBI agent hunting a calculating female serial killer. Bernstine’s attention-grabbing performance has emerged as a standout in one of the most buzzed-about new series of 2026."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Additionally, Starz will bestow on Bernstine’s award a special Starz #TakeTheLead designation as part of its ongoing commitment to amplifying narratives by, about, and for women and underrepresented audiences."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Emerging filmmakers Arie Esiri and Chuko Esiri will receive the Breakthrough Director Award for Neon’s Clarissa , a reimagining of Virginia Woolf’s Mrs. Dalloway set in contemporary Lagos, Nigeria. article_text:
It is a star-studded lineup for the Critics Choice Association’s ninth annual Celebration of Black Cinema & Television.

Debbie Allen , Chris Rock , Quinta Brunson , Jaafar Jackson and Chiwetel Ejiofor are among this year’s honorees for this year’s event, taking place November 16 and highlighting standout performances and work, both onscreen and offscreen, from the Black entertainment community. Roy Wood Jr. hosts the show.

Related Stories

2026-27 Awards Season Calendar: Oscars, Emmys, Grammys, Guilds & More

Taraji P. Henson Encourages Artists To ‘Knock Down’ Walls, Sarah Finn Celebrates Casting Community & More At 2026 Newport Beach Film Festival Honors

“We are proud to announce that the celebration continues,” said Shawn Edwards, executive producer and writer of the Critics Choice Association’s Celebration of Black Cinema & Television. “At a time when there has been a direct assault on Black culture and Black history, the Critics Choice Association stands firmly committed to recognizing the best in Black cinema and television. This isn’t something that we have to do, it’s something that we want to do. Creating a space where these bold and visionary storytellers can come together for an evening and be honored is our privilege and something that we are firmly committed to doing each year.”

Honorees for this year’s Celebration of Black Cinema & Television will include, per the CCA:

Watch on Deadline

Academy Honorary Award recipient, six-time Emmy winner, and two-time Tony nominee Debbie Allen will receive the Icon Award, recognizing her extraordinary career and enduring cultural impact across nearly five decades, with more than 140 acting, producing, and directing credits. Her tribute will celebrate the legacy of A Different World and its 2026 Netflix sequel, bringing the Black college experience to a new generation. Allen produced the original series and directed 83 of its 144 episodes, helping shape a groundbreaking show that addressed HIV, colorism, and racism. She returns as executive producer and director of the sequel and reprises her role as Dr. Langhorne. The series has already been renewed for a second season.

Two-time Emmy Award winner and Critics Choice Award winner Quinta Brunson will receive the Groundbreaker Award for creating, executive producing, and starring in ABC’s Abbott Elementary , which premiered its sixth season on Oct. 7. Produced by Warner Bros. Television & 20th Television, the hit comedy has earned 37 Emmy nominations to date. Brunson made Emmy history in 2022 as the first solo Black woman to win for comedy writing, and in 2024 she became the first Black actress in more than 40 years to win Outstanding Lead Actress in a Comedy Series.

Academy Award and Critics Choice Award nominee Chiwetel Ejiofor will receive the Vanguard Award for his work in A24’s psychological horror film Backrooms . Directed by Kane Parsons, the horror hit opened to $81.4 million domestically, shattering the previous record for an A24 opening weekend release and becoming its highest-grossing film to date, earning more than $400 million worldwide. Ejiofor leads the cast alongside Renate Reinsve in the adaptation of Parsons’ viral YouTube series.

Emmy and Grammy Award winner Chris Rock will receive the Director Award for A24’s Misty Green . The film marks Rock’s fourth narrative feature as a director. He also wrote, produced, and co-stars in the film, which stars Rosalind Eleazar ( Slow Horses) in a career-defining turn portraying an actress fighting to revive her career.

Emmy Award winner Lamorne Morris will receive the Comedy Award for his work as Robbie Robertson in Prime Video’s superhero series Spider-Noir. The series earned 11 Emmy nominations, and won five Emmy Awards.

Pulitzer Prize winner Katori Hall will be honored with the Showrunner Award for Starz’s P-Valley . The series returns December 4 for its third and final season with a two-episode premiere. Hall created the series from her own play and directed both premiere episodes. P-Valley is Starz’s best-performing current original, with Season 2 averaging 11.6 million multiplatform viewers.

Jaafar Jackson will receive the Actor Award – Film for his critically acclaimed, crowd-pleasing portrayal of Michael Jackson in Lionsgate’s biographical film Michael , which marks his acting debut. The film set records not only for a music biopic—it became the first biopic of any kind to gross more than $1 billion worldwide and is the most successful release in Lionsgate history.

Emmy Award nominee Anthony Mackie will be honored with the Actor Award – Series for his work in Apple TV’s upcoming 12 12 12 , which he also executive produces. Mackie plays a disgraced FBI agent locked in a cat-and-mouse game across Europe with Jamie Dornan’s career criminal, in the eight-episode heist drama. 12 12 12 premieres globally on Apple TV on Nov. 13.

Emmy nominee Stephan James will be honored with the Supporting Actor Award – Film for his portrayal of Carl Weathers in Amazon MGM Studios’ I Play Rocky . Directed by Academy Award winner Peter Farrelly, the film chronicles the making of the original Rocky and Sylvester Stallone’s determination to write and star in it. The biographical drama opens in November.

Tony Award winner and Academy Award and Emmy nominee Sophie Okonedo will receive the Supporting Actress Award – Film for her performance in Independent Film Company’s coming-of-age drama Mouse , directed by Kelly O’Sullivan and Alex Thompson. The drama premiered at the Berlin Film Festival and begins its theatrical engagements next month.

SAG Award and Critics Choice Award nominee Ato Essandoh will receive the Supporting Actor Award – Series for his work as Stuart Hayford in Netflix’s drama series The Diplomat. The political thriller was nominated for Outstanding Drama Series at the Emmys in 2025 and again in 2026, and returned for its fourth season October 15.

Tony Award nominee Quincy Tyler Bernstine will receive the Supporting Actress Award – Series for her work as Nora Washington in Hulu’s Furious . Created by Elizabeth Meriwether, the thriller follows an FBI agent hunting a calculating female serial killer. Bernstine’s attention-grabbing performance has emerged as a standout in one of the most buzzed-about new series of 2026.

Additionally, Starz will bestow on Bernstine’s award a special Starz #TakeTheLead designation as part of its ongoing commitment to amplifying narratives by, about, and for women and underrepresented audiences.

Emerging filmmakers Arie Esiri and Chuko Esiri will receive the Breakthrough Director Award for Neon’s Clarissa , a reimagining of Virginia Woolf’s Mrs. Dalloway set in contemporary Lagos, Nigeria. The film stars fellow Celebration of Black Cinema & Television honoree Okonedo alongside David Oyelowo, Ayo Edebiri, India Amarteifio and Toheeb Jimoh. It premiered in the Directors’ Fortnight section of the 2026 Cannes Film Festival, becoming only the second Nigerian feature ever selected by the festival and opens in select theaters December 11.

Jaalen Best will be honored with the Rising Star Award for his performance as Cassius Clay in Prime Video’s Muhammad Ali biographical drama series, The Greatest . It is the first authorized scripted series about Ali’s life, with executive producers including his widow Lonnie Ali, as well as Josh Wakely and Michael B. Jordan. The series premieres on Prime Video on November 4.

The Critics Choice Association’s Celebration of Black Cinema & Television will be produced by Madelyn Hammond, Javier Infante and Ella Carlson of Hammond Infante Productions.

article_text:
RE:AL REIWAROMAN Documentary of RE:IWAROMAN

劇場公開日： 2026年10月23日

解説・あらすじ

「M-1グランプリ」で史上初の2連覇を果たした漫才コンビ・令和ロマンのくるまと松井ケムリが、7年ぶりの単独ライブ「RE:IWAROMAN」に挑むまでの数カ月間に密着したドキュメンタリー（「RE:IWAROMAN」Blu-ray／DVDに収録されたドキュメンタリー映像）。 2026年5月16日、2万席の音楽アリーナ・Kアリーナ横浜で開催された「RE:IWAROMAN」は、一般チケットが即日完売。当日は1万8063人が会場を埋め、全国120館のライブビューイングに7110人、オンライン配信に1万5146人が加わり、延べ約4万人が一夜を見つめた。カメラが追うのは、完成したステージからは見えない「つくる時間」。新作漫才6本をかたちにしていくネタ作りの過程と、チャンピオンとして表現に向き合う2人の葛藤から、令和ロマンの再出発を映し出す。 ナレーションを畑中ふうが担当し、ヤーレンズ、大王、博多華丸・大吉、男気サトシ、ベッキー、佐久間宣行らが出演。大野陽平（大野映像研究所）がディレクター・撮影、Takumi Katsuradaが企画・製作総指揮を務めた。2026年10月23日～29日にアップリンク吉祥寺で限定上映。

article_text:
Er kam mitten im Krieg in den Iran zurück – trotz einer anstehenden Haftstrafe. Nun geht die iranische Justiz weiter gegen den Starregisseur Jafar Panahi vor

Der renommierte iranische Regisseur Jafar Panahi ist einem Bericht zufolge zu einer weiteren mehrjährigen Haftstrafe verurteilt worden. Ein Revolutionsgericht in der Hauptstadt Teheran habe ihn zu fünf Jahren und einem Monat Gefängnis verurteilt, berichtete die Zeitung "Emtedad" unter Berufung auf Panahis Anwalt Mostafa Nili. Außerdem soll sein gesamtes Vermögen beschlagnahmt werden. Darüber hinaus sei eine zweijährige Ausreisesperre verhängt worden.

Der 66-Jährige war Anfang April mitten im Krieg zurück in seine Heimat gereist. "Vergangene Woche teilte mein Mandant mit, dass seine Bankkonten gesperrt wurden", sagte Nili der Zeitung. Seine Nachforschungen bei der Justiz hatten dann aufgedeckt, dass Panahi in Abwesenheit verurteilt worden war.

Zuvor hatte die iranische Justiz den Starregisseur wegen "Propaganda gegen das System" bereits zu einem Jahr Haft verurteilt. Als zentralen Beweis führte ein Gericht seinen heimlich gedrehten Film "Ein einfacher Unfall" an. Das Werk gewann 2025 die Goldene Palme in Cannes und war zudem für die Golden Globes und die Oscars nominiert.

Panahi gilt seit Jahren als prominenter Kritiker im Iran. Er war von Juli 2022 bis Februar 2023 inhaftiert. Seit Jahren unterliegt er Einschränkungen bei beruflicher Tätigkeit und Reisen.

editorial_title_zh: 格奥尔格·巴塞利茨：英雄们 评论——令人惊叹的画作对历史发起猛烈一击
editorial_excerpt_zh: Thaddaeus Ropac 画廊，伦敦 这位艺术家捕捉了德国纳粹过往带来的恐惧、厌恶与罪责。其巨大尺幅的成果讽刺得如此尖刻，仿佛被人啐了一口。当德国画家格奥尔格·巴塞利茨今年去世时，欧洲正迅速消退的历史记忆也随之失去了一大块……
